newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ market unfazed by prospect of extra debt supply.
newsitem.headline: NZ market unfazed by prospect of extra debt supply.

text.p: The New Zealand bond market is well placed to take in its stride any increased supply that could stem from an increase in the government bond tender programme within the 1997/98 budget, analysts said on Wednesday.

Treasurer Winston Peters, due to release details of the 1997/98 programme in Thursday's budget, sent a chill through financial markets late last week by saying they held too optimistic a view on the country's fiscal prospects.
He hinted that markets had underestimated the government's borrowing needs, and that budget surpluses would be smaller than previously flagged.
In 1996/97 the government's bond tender programme was worth NZ$1.3 billion ($890 million), including $300 million inflation-indexed bonds (IIBs).

Economists have now revised up their expectations for the size of the 1997/98 programme to around NZ$1.5 billion from $1 billion. Some expect as much as $2 billion of new nominal bonds, but remain confident the tenders will be well supported.

"Even if it's $2 billion it's not exactly sizeable. It's only six or seven hundred (million) more than last year, and last year most tenders went pretty well," a Wellington senior dealer told Reuters.

"If anything, for the holders of paper offshore it's probably actually a positive, in terms of liquidity and the commitment to maintaining a benchmark -- as long as they issue a new 10-year," he said.
Most dealers expect the announcement of a new bond, maturing in 2008 or 2009, which would become the 10-year benchmark.
An Auckland bond dealer said Peters' signal that the bond programme would exceed that of 1996/97 had shocked the market.

"The comment is causing people to revise their numbers up dramatically, but personally I'd expect something just a little bit bigger than last year. They don't really need the money, so it's more a matter of continuity in the market," he said.

"But the potential supply of $1.2 or $1.5 billion over a year is not that large for a market to cope with...given the offshore demand we're seeing at the moment, I think the market is comfortable we can cope with that," he said.

Bankers Trust New Zealand now sees NZ$2 billion of nominal bonds and a further $250 million IIBs. But its economist Nick Bennenbroek noted even if BTNZ's forecast proved right, net supply would be unchanged because around $2 billion of July 1997 bonds were due to roll off shortly.

Bennenbroek said BTNZ expected all of the new nominal bonds to be the new 10-year benchmark, which would make it a reasonably liquid issue by the end of the fiscal year. He said the IIBs would probably be more 2016s, as in 1996/97.
A Wellington dealer said a programme worth $1.5 billion might provoke some knee-jerk bond selling but it would be shor bt-lived.
Even combined with bad news in the budget about lower surpluses and higher government spending, a higher bond programme would not see the market sell too far or for any length of time.

Dealers expect some steepening of the New Zealand yield curve if the government meets market expectations by announcing a new 10-year benchmark bond, which would increase supply in the longer maturities, lowering prices and raising yields. ($=NZ$1.46)
